newsitem.title: SPAIN: ETA rebels convicted of trying to kill Spain king.
newsitem.headline: ETA rebels convicted of trying to kill Spain king.

text.p: Three Basque guerrillas who said they had Spain's King Juan Carlos in their rifle sights three times have been convicted of plotting to kill him and sentenced to a total of 109 years in prison, judicial officials said on Monday.

The Spanish High Court announced its verdict on the same day the rebels, after a week of nationwide anti-ETA protests, struck back with a grenade attack near a police station in northern Spain, slightly injuring one person.

As some Basque separatist prisoners broke ranks and joined in condemning the ETA guerrilla group's killing on July 12 of a young politician, one rebel inmate was found hanged in his jail cell in central Spain in an apparent suicide, Interior Ministry officials said.
Officials welcomed the court verdict at a time when sentiment against separatist violence was running high.

The court handed down long prison sentences against Juan Jose Rego, his son Ignacio Rego and Jorge Garcia for "crimes against the Crown, belonging to an armed band and terrorist activities using arms of war and explosives".

The trial attracted widespread interest among Spaniards when it started in Madrid on January 22. The popular King Juan Carlos cemented his role as guardian of Spain's young democracy when he helped thwart a 1981 coup attempt.

In dramatic testimony, two of the three men charged -- Juan Jose Rego and Garcia -- told how they rented a flat on the Mediterranean island of Mallorca with a direct line of vision to the king's sailing yacht and how they had him in their gunsight.
Garcia told the court he did not shoot the king because escape plans had not been finalised.

He and Juan Jose Rego described Juan Carlos, Crown Prince Felipe and Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar as "prime targets" for ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom), which has killed 800 people in a nearly 30-year struggle for Basque independence.
The conviction comes a week after the separatist rebels brutally killed 29-year-old Miguel Angel Blanco, sparking national outrage.

In the wake of the killing and the massive street protests that surrounded it, the government promised to speed up trials of ETA suspects and make legislative reforms to close legal loopholes exploited by the guerrillas.
Spanish and French ministers met on Monday and agreed to step up joint efforts to hunt down and capture ETA's leaders, who police say operate out of France's southern Basque region.
"This savage form of violence cannot be justified in democratic countries," French Interior Minister Jean Pierre Chevenement told reporters.
Aznar offered an olive branch to people in the radical separatist movement who were having second thoughts after the latest attacks.

"The best decision that they can take is to leave violence, and they will find a hand held out to them," Aznar told a news conference after meeting the slain politician's fellow Basque town councillors.
"There will not be hateful nor vengeful attitudes on my part, always in a climate of coherence and under the law," he said.
